title: Bil-maṭ‘am — eating out
goal: Order food from a menu, ask about ingredients and flavor, ask for the bill, and understand the polite phrases around eating.
bekal: order a full meal from starters to dessert
ask what's in a dish and whether it's spicy or halal
ask for the bill and pay with the right phrases

dialogs.title: حَكِي — مَطْعَم شَعْبِي
dialogs.intro: A simple restaurant in Damascus. Budi and Laila sit down and the waiter brings the menu.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: What's in it? Is it spicy?

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.text: لَا، مِش حَارّ. دَجَاج وْبَصَل وْسُمَّاق.
lines.baca: la’, mish haarr. dajaaj w baṣal w summaa’.
lines.id: It's not spicy. Chicken, onion, and sumac.
lines.literal: no, not hot. chicken and onion and sumac.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.baca: ṭayyib, baddi waahid. w mazze kamaan.
lines.id: OK, I'll have one. And some mezze too.
lines.literal: good, want-I one. and mezze also.

lines.speaker: اَلْجَرْسُون:
lines.text: أَيّ مَزَّة؟ عِنَّا حُمُّص وْمْتَبَّل وْتَبُّولِة.
lines.baca: ayy mazze? ‘inna hummuṣ w mtabbal w tabbuule.
lines.id: Which mezze? We have hummus, mutabbal, and tabbouleh.
lines.literal: which mezze? at-us hummus and mutabbal and tabbouleh.

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.baca: w ana baddi fattuush w shiish ṭaawuu’.
lines.id: I'd like fattoush and shish tawook.
lines.literal: and I want-I fattoush and shish tawook.

lines.speaker: اَلْجَرْسُون:
lines.id: What would you like to drink?

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: An ayran for me, and water for the table.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: Excuse me, is the chicken halal?

lines.speaker: اَلْجَرْسُون:
lines.id: Of course. Everything here is halal.

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.id: After the meal, the bill, please.

notes: **The word مَزَّة is the key to eating in the Levant.** It means a spread of small dishes eaten together before, or instead of, a main course — hummus, mutabbal, tabbouleh, fattoush, and dozens more. Ordering three or four مَزَّة for two people is completely normal.
**The phrase شُو فِيه؟ means "what's in it?"** Literally "what inside it," it's the most useful question in this unit. For a feminine dish, the form is شُو فِيهَا؟
**The word حَارّ means spicy, not hot in temperature.** For temperature, use سُخْن. Levantine food is mostly **not spicy** — if you want heat, ask for شَطَّة (chili sauce) on the side.

**Asking about halal is perfectly normal and not offensive.** In Syria and Jordan almost all meat is halal; in Lebanon, it depends on the area. A more targeted question is فِي لَحِم خِنْزِير؟ ("is there pork?") rather than asking in general.

**The phrase عَ رَاسِي literally means "on my head."** It means "sure, with pleasure," like حَاضِر but warmer. Together with مِن عْيُونِي and تَكْرَم عَيْنَك, these are the Levantine ways of saying "you got it."
**The word لَإِلِي means "for me."** It combines لَـ (for) with a possessive ending. Other forms: لَإِلَك، لَإِلِك، لَإِلُو، لَإِلَا. If that feels complicated, you can just say أَنَا بَدِّي…

grammars.title: Ordering: four patterns
after: To say how many portions, put the number in front with no extra word: تْلَات حُمُّص means "three hummus." You don't need a word like "portion" or "plate" unless you want to stress it.
To cancel or change an order: لَحْظَة، غَيَّرِت رَأْيِي *lahẓa, ghayyart ra’yi* ("one moment, I changed my mind"). That's perfectly fine as long as the order hasn't come out yet.

grammars.title: Adjectives for food
after: The word طَيِّب does double duty again: as an adjective it means "good, tasty," and as an exclamation it means "OK then," as in unit 3. The context always makes it clear.

To praise someone's cooking, the must-say phrase is تِسْلَم إِيدَيْك *tislam iidēk* ("bless your hands") to a man or تِسْلَم إِيدَيْكِي to a woman. It's not small talk — skipping it comes across as ungrateful.

blocks.text: The dish مَنْسَف has a special place in Jordan: it's not just food but a mark of honor, served at big occasions and eaten together from one platter. If you're invited to a مَنْسَف, it's not an invitation to turn down.

blocks.title: Three things that surprise newcomers
items: **Bread, not rice, is the staple.** Bread (خُبْز) comes with every meal without being ordered.
**Eating with your right hand is completely normal**, especially for mezze and bread. Cutlery is there, but optional.
**Portions are big and your host will keep adding more.** Answer their صَحْتَين with عَ قَلْبَك, and to stop, say خَلَص، شَبْعِت، اَللَّه يْخَلِّيك.

head: Levantine
Say it
Meaning
rows: bless your hands (the cooking was great)
reply to praise for the food

blocks.text: The word دَايْمًا literally means "always," and hosts say it when guests praise the food — roughly "may this table always be full." The full form is سُفْرَة دَايْمِة, and hearing it means you've been made welcome.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Who pays
items: In the Levant, whoever invites usually pays for everyone, and arguing over the bill is part of the expected politeness.
If you really want to pay, tell the waiter early, not at the table. If you lose the argument, accept with اَللَّه يْخَلِّيك and offer to pay next time: اَلْمَرَّة الْجَايِة عَلَيِّي.
A tip of about ten percent is usual in restaurants, and not expected at small cafés or street stalls.

exercises.prompt: Match each description with its dish. Write the name of the dish in Arabic.
Put the words in the right order.
